beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Boopesh M., and this video is about Deep Hedging, a 2019 paper by Buehler, Gonon, Teichmann and Wood, from J P Morgan and E T H Zurich. Quick note: this is an AI voice reading my script. And every number you'll see comes from my own small replication, not from the paper.

beats.role_note: BLUF -- hesitant writer corrects the misconception
beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one line. The textbook hedge is exact, but only if trading is free. And in real markets, trading is never free.

props.text: Black–Scholes tells you exactly how to hedge.
props.replacementWords: how to hedge, if trading is free

contextItems.label: Textbook
contextItems.detail: rebalance all the time, at zero cost

beats.narration_text: Say you sell a call option on a stock trading at a hundred dollars, expiring in thirty trading days. To cancel the risk, you hold delta shares of the stock. Black-Scholes gives delta as N of d one: a number between zero and one that moves with the price. The rule is to adjust it every trading day.

beats.role_note: turnover and fees of the daily delta hedge, from results.json
beats.narration_text: But in real markets, every trade pays a fee. I set it to half a percent. Over the month, the daily delta hedge trades about two point two shares per option, and pays a dollar eleven in fees. The option only sold for two seventy-five. That's about forty percent, gone.

beats.role_note: the paper's move: learned policy, objective incl. costs, entropic utility
beats.narration_text: Deep Hedging's move is simple. Let a small neural network choose the position each day, from the time left, the price, and what it already holds. Then train it on simulated paths to maximise a score of the final profit that includes the fees. For the score, I use the entropic utility from Buehler's own code: big losses count much more than small ones.

beats.role_note: P&L histograms BS vs deep under costs + stats table
beats.narration_text: Here's the result on forty thousand fresh test paths, with the half-percent fee. Grey is the Black-Scholes delta, teal is the deep hedge. On average, the seller loses a dollar eleven with Black-Scholes, and sixty-five cents with the deep hedge. The spread is wider, but the worst five percent of outcomes improve, and so does the risk score it was trained to maximise.

beats.role_note: one path: positions BS vs deep; turnover and fee bars
beats.narration_text: So what did it learn? Here's one test path. Black-Scholes nudges its position every single day. The deep hedge moves more smoothly, and skips the small back-and-forth that the fee would punish. Across all the test paths, it trades one point three shares instead of two point two, and pays sixty-five cents in fees instead of a dollar eleven.

Is it fooling itself? Sanity check: set the fee to zero, and the network should rediscover Black-Scholes. It nearly does. Its positions differ by about two hundredths of a share on average, and its utility is slightly worse. Now the limits. This is a toy world: Black-Scholes prices, one option. The paper goes further, with S and P five hundred data and the Heston model. And a learned hedge is only as good as the simulator it trained on. Small network, one fee level.

Your turn. Paste this into Claude, with my script attached. Double the fee to one percent and retrain. Does the network trade even less, and does it still beat the Black-Scholes delta? A good answer shows the numbers, not just a story.
